The main syllable receives heavier stress, the presyllables lighter stress. When two presyllables occur the one just before the main syllable is more lightly stressed. Using PS for presyllable and MS for main syllable the phonological word is formulated as: ((PS2)PS1)MS.' -- the reported quot…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The Chru phonological word is a word-final main syllable preceded by up to two presyllables; stress falls on the final (main) syllable. Presyllables are weakly stressed and have only schwa or /a/ as vowels (sec.5.1, p.84).
new_statements.secondary_stress: With two presyllables, the first (word-initial) presyllable is less weak than the one immediately before the main syllable, i.e. relative prominence PS2 > PS1, both lighter than MS. No formal secondary-stress category.
new_statements.exceptions: None. Stress is not described as contrastive. Sec.6 (p.85) notes a separate non-contrastive breathy/clear register feature.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'phonological word' (max. three syllables, e.g. pətərbla' 'to turn over'); statement is about word-level citation forms, not phrasal prominence. Corroborated by Brunelle et al. 2020:6 ('final stressed syllable (the main syllable)', presyllable 'unstressed').
new_statements.identity_note: Fuller 1977 describes the speech of Diom village, Don Duong district (then Tuyen Duc province, now Lam Dong); one example (n.8) is flagged as Jut-Madan dialect. Brunelle et al. 2020 recorded in Diom A and Proh, same district. Both are Chru proper (chru1239); no separate dialect glottocode. The Glottolog ref Doke 1923-26 (ch~unduru Bushmen) is a misattribution and irrelevant.

new_statements.quote: Target syllables were always stressed and in word-final position. In most words, an unstressed syllable preceded the target syllable (44/60).
new_statements.citation: Brunelle, M., Ta Thanh Tan, Kirby, J. & Dinh Lu Giang. 2019. Obstruent devoicing and registrogenesis in Chru. In Proceedings of the 19th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, Melbourne.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (5 pp., text, printed pages 517-521 confirmed from page footers). Fresh extracted text of PDF page 2 (printed p. 518), section '2.1. Experiment', reads exactly: 'Target syllables were always stressed and in word-final position. In most words, an unstressed syllable preceded the target syllable (44/60).' -- verbatim match to the compiler quote. The section describes the 60-word stimulus list (coronal/velar onsets + five long vowels); the stress sentence is incidental to stimulus design, not a prosody description, and the compiler says so. An independent a full-text search for stress/accent the PDF for stress/accent/prominence/syllable finds no other stress statement (the other 'syllab…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (final stress, final) and as Fuller 1977 p.77 (main syllable = final, heavier stress; presyllables lighter). The 2019 paper restates in passing what its 2020 LabPhon sequel (already held by the project, p.6 sec.2.1.1) also says: the final main syllable is the stressed one and the presyllable is unstressed. Adds no detail on weight, secondary stress or exceptions.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the word-final main syllable; a preceding (pre)syllable, where present, is unstressed. Stated only as a property of the elicited stimuli (60 real words), not as a general phonological rule, but the authors treat final stress as the norm for the language.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (Fuller 1977 calls presyllable stress 'lighter'; this paper calls the preceding syllable simply 'unstressed').
new_statements.exceptions: None. The paper is an instrumental study of the voicing-to-register transition (f0, F1, voice quality, VOT); it has no phonology or prosody section and no further stress statement anywhere in the text (a full-text search for stress/accent/prominence/tone). It treats Chru as a register language, not a tone language, following Fuller [8:85] on non-contrastive register.
new_statements.identity_note: Brunelle et al. 2019 recorded 26 speakers in the villages of Diom A and Proh, Don Duong district, Lam Dong province (p. 517-518) — the same Don Duong area as Fuller 1977 (Diom village dialect) and the same speaker pool as Brunelle et al. 2020 (LabPhon). No dialect divergence on stress is reported.

sources.note: Comparative: in Chru and Rade the pretonic syllable shows no vocalic contrasts (only schwa); Chru has reduced only some iambic disyllables to monosyllables. No Chru-specific stress rule beyond the Chamic iambic/final-main-syllable frame.
